slides.say: The figure shows a regular octagon. K L and M N are perpendicular, and they meet at T. K, L, M and N are corners of the octagon. Sara says that L T is bigger than two times K T. Ben says that the perimeter of triangle K M T is equal to M N. Which of the following is true?
at: The figure shows a regular octagon
The figure shows a regular octagon

slides.say: Whatever way we choose, the first step is the octagon cut from the lesson. K L and M N are already two of its lines. Let's draw the other two. Now we have a square in the middle, four rectangles, and four silver triangles in the corners. K M T is one of the corner triangles.
at: K M T is one of the corner triangles

slides: We'll solve it in two different ways, by plugging in numbers, and then by understanding.

slides.say: Let's plug in numbers. We could choose the octagon's side. But then, to get K T, we'd have to divide by root two. It's easier to multiply. So let's choose K T, a leg of the corner triangle. The easiest number is one.
Triangle K M T is a silver triangle, so its legs are equal, and M T is one too. The hypotenuse K M is the leg times root two, so it's root two.
K M is a side of the octagon. So every side of the octagon is root two, and so is the side of the square. And every corner triangle has legs of one.
at: So every side of the octagon

slides.say: Now Sara. L T goes from T down to L. It's the side of the square, root two, plus the leg of the bottom triangle, one. So L T is root two plus one. And two times K T is two times one, two.
at: L T goes from T down to L

slides.say: Which is bigger, root two plus one, or two? Let's take one away from both. That's root two against one. Root two is more than one, because two is more than one. So L T is bigger, and Sara is right. Choice number one, only Ben, is out. And choice number four, neither, is out too.
at: Root two is more than one

slides.say: Now Ben. The perimeter of triangle K M T is one, plus one, plus root two. That's two plus root two.
at: one, plus one, plus root two

slides.say: M N goes from M to N. First the leg M T, one. Then the side of the square, root two. Then the leg on the right, one. So M N is two plus root two too. They're equal, so Ben is right. Both are right. Choice number two is our answer.
at: M N goes from M to N
So M N is two plus root two

slides.say: Now by understanding, with no numbers at all. We just match equal pieces. Sara compares two times K T with L T. L T is the side of the square, plus the leg at the bottom. And that leg is equal to K T, because all the corner triangles are the same.
at: that leg is equal to K T

slides.say: So let's take one K T away from both sides. What's left? One K T for Sara's two times K T, and the side of the square for L T.

The side of the square is a side of the octagon, like the hypotenuse K M. And K T is only a leg. In a right triangle, the hypotenuse is the longest side. So L T is more than two times K T, and Sara is right.
at: The side of the square is a side
the hypotenuse is the longest side

slides.say: You could also see it in the figure. On the exam, a figure is not necessarily drawn to scale, so usually we don't rely on it. But a regular polygon is the exception. It can't be drawn any other way, so its figure is accurate. Measure the two lengths with your fingers, and you'll see that L T is longer than two times K T. That's only a quick check. The proof is what we just did, with the hypotenuse.
at: But a regular polygon is the exception

slides.say: Now Ben. The perimeter of K M T is K T plus M T plus K M. And M N is M T, plus the side of the square, plus the leg on the right.
at: The perimeter of K M T

slides.say: M T is on both sides, so it cancels. K M is a side of the octagon, the same as the side of the square. And K T is a leg, the same as the leg on the right. So the two are equal, and Ben is right too. Choice number two is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: M T is on both sides
Choice number two is our answer
